summary: Emergency department visit was billed at the highest acuity level using CPT 99285 (level 5). The medical record contained minimal documentation and did not support high-complexity medical decision-making or a life-threatening presentation. The facility fee for the ED visit was also substantially above typical benchmarks for this level of care.
recommended_actions: Request complete ED physician note; compare documented MDM complexity against level 5 criteria.
evidence_requests: ED physician note, triage assessment, nursing notes, vital signs flowsheet.
evidence_checklist: Does chart document high-complexity MDM?
Are vital signs consistent with level 5 acuity?
Is there a life-threatening condition documented?
Does the HPI support the level billed?
letter_snippet: The emergency visit was billed at the highest acuity level (99285), yet the available documentation does not support high-complexity medical decision-making or a life-threatening presentation as required for this code.
typical_outcome: Downgrade to 99284 or 99283 after records review.

summary: The bill contained a duplicate charge for the same complete blood count (CBC) lab panel, CPT 85025, on the same date of service in an outpatient setting. Only one lab draw and one panel were ordered and performed according to the clinical record. The duplicate line item should be identified and removed from the bill.
recommended_actions: Request itemized statement and compare line items; flag identical service on same date.
evidence_requests: Itemized bill, lab order requisition, lab results for date of service.
evidence_checklist: Are there two identical CPT 85025 charges on the same date?
Was only one lab panel ordered per the physician note?
Does the lab report show one result set or two?
letter_snippet: The bill includes duplicate charges for a complete blood count (CPT 85025) on the same date of service. Only one panel was ordered and performed, and the duplicate charge should be removed.
typical_outcome: Removal of the duplicate charge.

summary: Unbundled charges appeared on the bill for a surgical procedure: the wound closure and other components were billed separately even though they are normally included in the global surgical package for the primary procedure. NCCI edits indicate that CPT 12001 (wound closure) is bundled with the hernia repair code 49505. No modifier or documentation supported billing them as distinct procedures.
recommended_actions: Cross-reference NCCI edits; request operative note to confirm bundled vs. separate procedures.
evidence_requests: Operative report, anesthesia record, NCCI edit documentation.
evidence_checklist: Does NCCI indicate 12001 is bundled with 49505?
Was the wound closure a separate, distinct procedure?
Is modifier 59 or XS justified by documentation?
letter_snippet: The wound closure (CPT 12001) was billed separately from the hernia repair (CPT 49505), but NCCI edits indicate these services are bundled. No modifier or documentation supports billing them as distinct procedures.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the unbundled closure charge.

summary: An outpatient MRI of the knee, CPT 73721, was performed at a hospital-based imaging center and the facility fee was excessive compared to CMS outpatient rates and regional benchmarks. The same study at a freestanding imaging center would typically cost a fraction of the amount. Price transparency data and CMS OPPS rates can be used to dispute the facility fee.
recommended_actions: Compare facility fee against CMS outpatient rate and regional benchmarks.
evidence_requests: Facility fee breakdown, hospital chargemaster excerpt for CPT 73721, CMS OPPS rate sheet.
evidence_checklist: Is the facility fee more than 3x the Medicare OPPS rate?
Was the MRI performed at a hospital-based vs. freestanding center?
Are there transparency pricing disclosures available?
letter_snippet: The facility fee for the knee MRI (CPT 73721) substantially exceeds both the CMS outpatient rate and regional benchmarks for the same service at freestanding imaging centers.
typical_outcome: Negotiated reduction of facility fee to benchmark range.

summary: The electrocardiogram (EKG) interpretation fee, CPT 93010, was billed at approximately six times the median negotiated rate for this service. The amount materially exceeded both the CMS physician fee schedule and typical commercial payer benchmarks. No clinical justification was documented for the markup over the standard interpretation fee.
recommended_actions: Request interpretation report; compare billed amount to CMS fee schedule and payer median.
evidence_requests: EKG interpretation report, provider credentials, CMS physician fee schedule for 93010.
evidence_checklist: Is the interpretation fee above the 90th percentile of negotiated rates?
Does the interpretation report exist and contain clinical findings?
Was the interpretation performed by a qualified physician?
letter_snippet: The EKG interpretation fee (CPT 93010) of $875 materially exceeds the median negotiated rate benchmark of $140, representing a 6x markup without justification for the variance.
typical_outcome: Reduction to a rate within the payer's negotiated range.

summary: A single-view chest X-ray, CPT 71045, was performed and the facility charge was significantly above the expected payer spread for this service. The charge exceeded typical benchmarks when compared to CMS OPPS rates and published price transparency data for the same procedure. Facility fees for routine radiology can often be disputed using transparency and benchmark comparisons.
recommended_actions: Request price transparency data; compare to CMS OPPS and state benchmarks.
evidence_requests: Itemized charge for CPT 71045, hospital price transparency file, state rate comparison.
evidence_checklist: Is the charge above 3x the Medicare rate?
Does the hospital price transparency file list a lower negotiated rate?
Is this a hospital-based or freestanding radiology service?
letter_snippet: The facility charge for a single-view chest X-ray (CPT 71045) exceeds the expected payer spread for this service profile, as benchmarked against CMS rates and published transparency data.
typical_outcome: Partial write-off or adjustment to transparency-listed rate.

summary: A therapeutic IV push, CPT 96374, was billed separately from an infusion service, CPT 96365, even though both were administered during the same session. CMS infusion hierarchy rules generally require that when an IV push and an infusion occur in the same encounter, they be reported in a specific sequential manner rather than as fully separate line items. The medication administration record should be reviewed to confirm timing and applicability of the hierarchy rules.
recommended_actions: Review CMS infusion hierarchy rules; request medication administration record.
evidence_requests: Medication administration record (MAR), nursing notes, infusion start/stop times.
evidence_checklist: Were the IV push and infusion concurrent in the same session?
Does the MAR support separate, distinct administration times?
Are CMS infusion hierarchy rules being followed?
letter_snippet: The IV push (CPT 96374) was billed separately from the concurrent infusion (CPT 96365), but CMS infusion hierarchy rules require sequential reporting when services occur in the same session.
typical_outcome: Removal of the separately billed IV push charge.

summary: CT of the thorax with contrast, CPT 71260, was billed with both the technical component and the professional component at levels that far exceeded CMS-established rates. The combined fee was substantially above the sum of the typical facility (TC) and physician (PC) fees for this study. Documentation did not support any reason for the variance from standard rates, and the charge may be disputed using CMS fee schedules and regional benchmarks.
recommended_actions: Request TC/PC split breakdown; compare each to CMS physician and facility rates.
evidence_requests: Technical component charge, professional component charge, CT report, CMS fee schedule for 71260-TC and 71260-26.
evidence_checklist: Is the TC fee above the CMS OPPS rate by more than 200%?
Is the professional component above the CMS physician fee schedule?
Was contrast medically necessary per clinical documentation?
letter_snippet: The combined technical and professional fees for CT thorax with contrast (CPT 71260) total $3,560, far exceeding the CMS-established rates for both components. Documentation does not justify the variance.
typical_outcome: Reduction of both TC and PC to benchmark-aligned rates.

summary: Physical therapy evaluation was billed twice on two consecutive days using the high-complexity evaluation code CPT 97163, but the clinical record indicated that only one evaluation was actually performed. The notes for both dates did not show distinct evaluations with new assessments or treatment plans. A single referral and a single evaluation session support removal of the duplicate evaluation charge.
recommended_actions: Request PT evaluation notes for both dates; confirm whether two separate evaluations occurred.
evidence_requests: Physical therapy evaluation notes for both dates, referral order, scheduling records.
evidence_checklist: Do notes exist for both dates showing distinct evaluations?
Was only one referral order placed?
Are the documented findings identical across both dates?
letter_snippet: A high-complexity PT evaluation (CPT 97163) was billed on two consecutive dates, yet the clinical record supports only one evaluation session. The duplicate charge should be reversed.
typical_outcome: Removal of the duplicate evaluation charge.

summary: An established patient office visit was billed at level 5 (CPT 99215) instead of the supported level 3 (99213). The documentation did not support high-complexity medical decision-making or the time threshold required for 99215 under current E/M guidelines. The problem list, MDM elements, and either time or complexity criteria should be compared against the 2021 and later E/M level requirements to justify a downgrade to 99213.
recommended_actions: Request office visit note; compare documented elements against E/M level criteria for 2021+ guidelines.
evidence_requests: Office visit note, problem list, medication list, time documentation if time-based billing.
evidence_checklist: Does the note document high-complexity MDM (99215 criteria)?
If time-based, is total time documented and >40 min?
Does the problem addressed justify level 5 complexity?
Are there at least 2 chronic conditions with mild exacerbation?
letter_snippet: The office visit was billed as level 5 (99215) but the documentation supports, at most, a moderate-complexity visit (99213). Neither the MDM elements nor the documented time meet the threshold for 99215.
typical_outcome: Downgrade to 99213 with corresponding charge reduction.

summary: Surgical pathology, CPT 88305, was billed as a separate line item even though the tissue specimen was obtained during a procedure that is typically covered under the surgical global package. The total knee replacement (CPT 27447) global period normally includes routine pathology examination of tissue removed during the procedure. Payer policy and the operative note should be checked to confirm that the pathology charge is not duplicative of the global surgical fee.
recommended_actions: Check whether pathology is included in the surgical global package; request pathology report.
evidence_requests: Pathology report, operative note, global surgery package documentation.
evidence_checklist: Is pathology routinely included in the global surgical fee?
Was a separate, distinct pathology specimen processed?
Does the operative note reference a separate pathology order?
letter_snippet: Surgical pathology (CPT 88305) was billed separately from the total knee replacement (CPT 27447), but the specimen evaluation is typically included in the surgical global package per payer policy.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the separately billed pathology charge.

summary: A minor laceration repair in the emergency department, CPT 12002, was billed with a facility fee that far exceeded the professional (procedure) charge and also exceeded CMS OPPS facility rates for this code. Simple laceration repairs are relatively low-cost procedures, and the facility component was disproportionately high when compared to both the physician component and to established benchmarks. The facility fee can be disputed using CMS OPPS and chargemaster comparison data.
recommended_actions: Compare facility fee to the procedural charge and CMS facility rate for the repair.
evidence_requests: Itemized bill showing facility vs. professional charges, CMS OPPS rate for 12002.
evidence_checklist: Is the facility fee more than 2x the professional component?
Does the facility fee exceed CMS OPPS by more than 300%?
Was the laceration simple or complex per documentation?
letter_snippet: The facility fee associated with a simple laceration repair (CPT 12002) is disproportionately high relative to both the professional charge and CMS-established facility rates for this minor procedure.
typical_outcome: Facility fee reduced to align with CMS OPPS benchmark.

summary: Anesthesia services for the procedure were billed with time units that exceeded the documented surgical duration by a significant margin. The anesthesia start and stop times on the anesthesia record did not align with the operative report incision and closure times, and the additional time units were not supported by documentation. Billed anesthesia time should be reconciled with the operative report and anesthesia record to reduce the charge to the actual documented duration.
recommended_actions: Cross-reference anesthesia start/stop times with operative report; verify time unit calculation.
evidence_requests: Anesthesia record with start/stop times, operative report with incision/close times, post-anesthesia note.
evidence_checklist: Do anesthesia start/stop times match the operative report?
Are the billed time units consistent with actual duration?
Is there a pre/post anesthesia assessment documented?
letter_snippet: The billed anesthesia time for CPT 00140 exceeds the documented surgical duration by a significant margin. The anesthesia record does not support the additional time units claimed.
typical_outcome: Reduction of anesthesia time units to match documented surgical time.

summary: The bill contained two charges for urinalysis, CPT 81001, on the same date of service in the emergency department. The clinical record and lab results indicated that only one specimen was collected and one set of results was reported. Duplicate lab charges on the same date without documentation of a repeat or add-on order are a common billing error and the duplicate urinalysis charge should be removed.
recommended_actions: Request lab results and order history for date of service; confirm single vs. multiple specimens.
evidence_requests: Lab order, urinalysis results, nursing notes documenting specimen collection.
evidence_checklist: Were two separate urinalysis specimens collected?
Does the lab report show one or two result sets?
Was a repeat UA clinically indicated and documented?
letter_snippet: The bill contains duplicate urinalysis charges (CPT 81001) for the same date of service. The clinical record indicates only one specimen was collected and analyzed.
typical_outcome: Removal of the duplicate urinalysis charge.

summary: A hospital stay was billed at full inpatient rates using codes such as 99234 or 99235, but the medical record did not contain a formal inpatient admission order. The length of stay and clinical presentation were consistent with observation status rather than inpatient admission. Utilization review and the absence of a signed inpatient admission order support disputing the inpatient level of billing and requesting rebilling at the appropriate observation rate with a corresponding charge reduction.
recommended_actions: Request admission order and utilization review determination; verify observation vs. inpatient status.
evidence_requests: Admission order, utilization review determination, physician attestation of inpatient medical necessity.
evidence_checklist: Is there a signed inpatient admission order?
Does utilization review support inpatient vs. observation status?
Was the stay under 48 hours (typical observation threshold)?
Did the physician document inpatient medical necessity?
letter_snippet: The stay was billed at inpatient rates, but the medical record does not contain a formal inpatient admission order. The clinical presentation and stay duration are consistent with observation status.
typical_outcome: Rebilling at observation rate with corresponding charge reduction.

summary: Pulse oximetry, CPT 94760, was billed as a separate line item in addition to the emergency department evaluation and management (E/M) service, CPT 99284. Per NCCI bundling edits, pulse oximetry performed as part of routine vital sign monitoring during an ED visit is typically included in the E/M service and should not be billed separately unless there is documentation of a distinct, separately medically necessary monitoring period. The separate pulse oximetry charge may be disputed as bundled.
recommended_actions: Verify whether pulse oximetry is bundled per NCCI with the E/M code; check for modifier.
evidence_requests: ED nursing flowsheet, vital signs documentation, NCCI edit reference for 94760 and 99284.
evidence_checklist: Is CPT 94760 bundled with the ED E/M code per NCCI?
Was oximetry used for extended monitoring beyond routine vitals?
Is there documentation supporting a separate, distinct service?
letter_snippet: Pulse oximetry (CPT 94760) was billed separately from the ED visit (CPT 99284), but this service is routinely included in the E/M evaluation per NCCI bundling edits.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the separately billed pulse oximetry charge.

summary: Intravenous normal saline administration was billed with a supply charge (e.g., J7030) and an administration fee (CPT 96360) that together reflected an extreme markup over the wholesale acquisition cost of the saline. The supply charge alone exceeded the typical wholesale cost by approximately twenty times, which is inconsistent with reasonable and customary billing for routine IV fluids. Itemized supply charges and WAC reference data can be used to request a reduction to a reasonable multiple of cost.
recommended_actions: Compare supply charge to wholesale acquisition cost (WAC); request itemized supply charges.
evidence_requests: Itemized supply charges, wholesale acquisition cost reference, medication administration record.
evidence_checklist: Is the saline supply charge more than 10x WAC?
Is the IV administration fee within payer benchmarks?
Was the volume of saline administered clinically appropriate?
letter_snippet: The charge for IV normal saline (J7030) and its administration (CPT 96360) includes a supply markup that exceeds the wholesale acquisition cost by approximately 20 times, which is not consistent with reasonable billing practices.
typical_outcome: Supply charge reduced to a reasonable multiple of WAC.

summary: Both a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), CPT 80053, and a basic metabolic panel (BMP), CPT 80048, were billed on the same date of service. The BMP is a subset of the CMP: all analytes in the BMP are included in the CMP. Billing both panels when only one draw was performed and the CMP was ordered results in duplicate billing for the same tests. The BMP charge should be removed as it is subsumed by the CMP.
recommended_actions: Confirm that both panels were medically necessary; BMP is a subset of CMP.
evidence_requests: Lab orders, lab results for both panels, physician order documentation.
evidence_checklist: Is the BMP a subset of the CMP?
Were both panels ordered separately by the physician?
Do lab results show distinct additional analytes beyond CMP?
letter_snippet: Both a comprehensive metabolic panel (CPT 80053) and a basic metabolic panel (CPT 80048) were billed on the same date. The BMP is a subset of the CMP, making the separate charge duplicative.
typical_outcome: Removal of the BMP charge since it is subsumed by the CMP.

summary: Operating room time was billed for four hours, but the operative report clearly documented a procedure that took approximately ninety minutes from incision to closure. The anesthesia record and OR scheduling log did not support the additional billed time. Pre-operative and PACU time should not be included in billed OR time. The OR time charge should be reduced to match the documented procedure duration to avoid overpayment for time not actually spent in the operating room.
recommended_actions: Compare billed OR time with operative report start/end times; request anesthesia and OR logs.
evidence_requests: Operative report with incision/close times, OR scheduling log, anesthesia time record.
evidence_checklist: What are the documented incision and close times?
Does the OR log support the billed 4-hour duration?
Is pre-op and PACU time being charged as OR time?
Does anesthesia time corroborate the OR time?
letter_snippet: Operating room time was billed for 4 hours, but the operative report documents a 90-minute procedure. The excess billed time is not supported by the surgical or anesthesia records.
typical_outcome: OR time charges reduced to match documented procedure duration.

summary: An emergency department visit was billed at level 4 (CPT 99284), which implies moderate to high complexity, but the chief complaint was a straightforward ankle sprain. No imaging was ordered, no procedures were performed, and the patient was discharged with simple instructions. The documented history, examination, and medical decision-making were consistent with a lower-level visit (99282 or 99283). The level 4 charge is not supported by the clinical documentation and may be downgraded with a corresponding reduction in the billed amount.
recommended_actions: Request ED note; compare documented acuity against level 4 criteria.
evidence_requests: ED physician note, triage assessment, discharge instructions, radiology orders if any.
evidence_checklist: Does the chief complaint support moderate-severity (level 4)?
Were any diagnostic tests or imaging performed?
Does the MDM support moderate complexity?
Was the patient discharged with simple instructions?
letter_snippet: The ED visit was billed at level 4 (99284) for a straightforward ankle sprain with no imaging ordered and a simple discharge. The documented presentation and MDM are consistent with a lower-level visit (99282 or 99283).
typical_outcome: Downgrade to 99282 or 99283 with corresponding reduction.

summary: An urgent care visit was billed as a high-complexity office visit (99215) when the encounter was a simple same-day evaluation for a minor illness. The note did not document multiple chronic conditions, high-complexity MDM, or extended time. Urgent care encounters are often over-leveled when compared to 2021 E/M criteria; the visit more closely matched 99213 or 99214.
recommended_actions: Request urgent care note; apply E/M level criteria and time if time-based.
evidence_requests: Urgent care encounter note, problem list, time documentation.
evidence_checklist: Does MDM meet 99215 criteria?
Was total time documented and >40 min?
Were 2+ chronic illnesses with exacerbation documented?
letter_snippet: The urgent care visit was billed at level 5 (99215) but the documentation supports a lower level (99213 or 99214). The E/M level should be adjusted to match the documented complexity and time.
typical_outcome: Downgrade to 99213 or 99214 with charge reduction.

summary: A sleep study (polysomnography) was billed twice for the same night—once as a full study and once as a split study or add-on—when only one continuous study was performed. The technician log and physician interpretation indicated a single night of monitoring. Duplicate sleep study billing is a known audit target when the same date of service appears for multiple sleep codes.
recommended_actions: Request sleep lab technician log and physician interpretation; confirm one night, one study.
evidence_requests: Sleep study report, technician worksheet, order for sleep study.
evidence_checklist: Was more than one full night of monitoring performed?
Does the report describe a split study with distinct portions?
Are both codes for the same date of service?
letter_snippet: The bill includes two sleep study charges for the same date of service. The record supports only one night of polysomnography. The duplicate charge should be removed.
typical_outcome: Removal of the duplicate sleep study charge.

summary: A screening colonoscopy was performed and a biopsy was taken; the biopsy (e.g., 88305 or 45380) was billed separately in addition to the colonoscopy with biopsy code (45380). When a biopsy is taken during a colonoscopy, the biopsy is typically included in the colonoscopy code or reported with a single appropriate code—not as a separate line item without proper modifier or distinct-site documentation.
recommended_actions: Verify NCCI and payer policy on colonoscopy with biopsy; request procedure note.
evidence_requests: Colonoscopy report, pathology report, order for biopsy.
evidence_checklist: Was the biopsy from the same site as the primary procedure?
Does payer policy bundle biopsy with 45380?
Is modifier 59 or distinct site documented?
letter_snippet: The biopsy was billed separately from the colonoscopy with biopsy (45380). Per NCCI and standard billing rules, the biopsy performed during the same procedure is not separately billable without distinct documentation.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the separately billed pathology or biopsy charge.

summary: A telehealth visit was billed with a place of service indicating an in-person office visit (e.g., 11) instead of telehealth (02), resulting in a higher facility or fee schedule application. The encounter was conducted via video and the record indicated telehealth; the place of service should be 02 and the appropriate telehealth modifier (e.g., 95) used to avoid incorrect payment or patient liability.
recommended_actions: Request encounter record and confirm place of service; ask for correction to POS 02 and modifier 95 if applicable.
evidence_requests: Encounter note indicating telehealth, platform used, place of service on claim.
evidence_checklist: Does the note state the visit was by video/telephone?
Was place of service 02 used?
Is modifier 95 or GT present if required?
letter_snippet: This encounter was conducted via telehealth, but the claim was submitted with a place of service for an in-person visit. The place of service should be corrected to 02 (telehealth) with the appropriate modifier.
typical_outcome: Reprocessing with correct POS and modifier; possible refund if patient overcharged.

summary: A drug was billed with a quantity of 10 units when only 1 or 2 units were administered according to the medication administration record (MAR) and the physician order. Unit-based drug billing (e.g., J-codes) is a common source of overbilling when the quantity is not reconciled with the actual dose and frequency documented in the chart.
recommended_actions: Compare billed quantity to MAR and physician order; request pharmacy dispensing record.
evidence_requests: MAR, physician order, pharmacy record, itemized drug charges.
evidence_checklist: What quantity was ordered?
What quantity appears on the MAR for the date of service?
Does the billed quantity match the dispensed and administered amount?
letter_snippet: The drug was billed for 10 units, but the medication administration record and order document only 1 (or 2) units administered. The quantity should be corrected to match the documented administration.
typical_outcome: Reduction of drug charge to reflect actual units administered.

summary: An injection (e.g., CPT 96372 or 96401) was billed in addition to an office visit on the same day without documentation that the injection was a significant, separate service. Modifier 25 was appended to the E/M, but the note did not describe a distinct E/M service beyond the injection. NCCI and payer policies often bundle the injection with the visit when the visit is solely for the injection.
recommended_actions: Review note for separate E/M; confirm modifier 25 criteria are met.
evidence_requests: Office visit note, injection documentation, modifier 25 justification.
evidence_checklist: Does the note document a separate E/M from the injection?
Was modifier 25 supported by documentation?
Would the E/M have been performed if no injection was given?
letter_snippet: The office visit (99213) and injection (96372) were both billed with modifier 25 on the E/M. The documentation does not support a significant, separately identifiable E/M service; the visit was for the injection only. The E/M charge should be removed or the modifier 25 reversed.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the E/M charge or removal of modifier 25.

summary: Critical care time (99291, 99292) was billed for 60 minutes, but the progress notes and flow sheet did not document continuous critical care or the required elements for critical care. The patient was in a step-down or general floor for part of the time, or the physician was not exclusively devoted to this patient. Critical care time must be well documented and meet CMS criteria.
recommended_actions: Request all progress notes and flow sheets for the date; verify continuous critical care and exclusivity.
evidence_requests: Critical care progress notes, nursing flow sheet, location/setting documentation.
evidence_checklist: Is the patient in an ICU or critical care setting?
Is time documented in continuous blocks?
Was the physician exclusively managing this patient during the time billed?
letter_snippet: Critical care (99291/99292) was billed for 60 minutes, but the documentation does not support continuous critical care time or exclusivity to this patient as required. The time billed should be reduced to match the documented critical care time.
typical_outcome: Reduction of critical care time units to documented time.

summary: Durable medical equipment (DME)—such as a CPAP supply or diabetic supplies—was billed at a price that far exceeded the Medicare allowable or typical retail price for the same item. DME markup is a frequent source of overcharges when the same product is available at a lower cost through other suppliers or when the billed amount is multiple times the Medicare fee schedule.
recommended_actions: Compare billed amount to Medicare fee schedule and retail; request itemized DME invoice.
evidence_requests: DME order, itemized invoice, Medicare fee schedule for HCPCS code.
evidence_checklist: What is the Medicare allowable for this HCPCS code?
Is the billed amount more than 2–3x the allowable?
Was the item actually received by the patient?
letter_snippet: The DME charge for this supply exceeds the Medicare allowable and typical market price for the same item. The charge should be reduced to a reasonable and customary amount.
typical_outcome: Reduction of DME charge to fee schedule or negotiated rate.

summary: A cardiac stress test (e.g., treadmill or pharmacologic) was performed in a hospital outpatient department and the facility fee was several times higher than the same test at a freestanding cardiology office or independent diagnostic facility. Facility fees for stress tests vary widely by setting; transparency data and CMS rates can support a dispute when the hospital-based fee is disproportionate.
recommended_actions: Compare facility fee to CMS OPPS and freestanding rates; request price transparency data.
evidence_requests: Itemized facility and professional charges, CMS OPPS for stress test, transparency file.
evidence_checklist: Is the facility fee above 3x the Medicare OPPS rate?
Was the test in a hospital vs. freestanding lab?
Does the transparency file show a lower negotiated rate?
letter_snippet: The facility fee for the cardiac stress test substantially exceeds the CMS outpatient rate and the typical rate at freestanding facilities. We request a reduction to a benchmark-aligned amount.
typical_outcome: Negotiated reduction of facility fee.

summary: A spinal injection (e.g., epidural or facet) was billed with a separate charge for fluoroscopic guidance (77003) or for the injection at multiple levels when the documentation supported a single-level injection with guidance included. NCCI and payer policies often bundle image guidance into the primary injection code or limit levels without distinct documentation.
recommended_actions: Check NCCI edits for injection and guidance; request procedure note and imaging report.
evidence_requests: Procedure note, fluoroscopy report, order for injection.
evidence_checklist: Is image guidance bundled with the injection code per NCCI?
How many levels were injected per the note?
Is there documentation for separate billing of guidance?
letter_snippet: Fluoroscopic guidance (77003) was billed separately from the spinal injection, but guidance is typically included in the primary injection code. The separate guidance charge should be removed.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the separately billed guidance or level.

summary: A well-child visit (e.g., 99391–99395) was billed along with vaccine administration (90460, 90461) and vaccine product codes as if the vaccines were not part of the preventive visit. Some payers bundle vaccine administration into the well-child visit when performed at the same encounter; duplicate administration fees or incorrect packaging can result in overbilling.
recommended_actions: Verify payer policy on well-child and vaccine admin; request encounter note and vaccine log.
evidence_requests: Well-child note, vaccine administration record, immunization schedule.
evidence_checklist: Does the payer bundle vaccine admin with the preventive visit?
Were multiple admin fees billed for a single encounter?
Is the vaccine product separately billable per policy?
letter_snippet: The well-child visit and vaccine administration were billed in a way that duplicates services included in the preventive visit. We request a review and removal of any duplicate administration or visit charges.
typical_outcome: Removal of duplicate admin or adjustment per payer policy.

summary: A dialysis treatment was billed twice for the same date when the patient received only one session. Dialysis billing is typically once per session per day; duplicate line items for the same date can indicate a billing error or a duplicate claim that should be voided.
recommended_actions: Request dialysis run sheet and treatment record for the date; confirm one session.
evidence_requests: Dialysis treatment record, run sheet, order for dialysis.
evidence_checklist: How many dialysis sessions were documented for this date?
Does the run sheet show one or two runs?
Was the patient admitted or had a second session at another facility?
letter_snippet: The bill shows two dialysis charges for the same date of service. The treatment record indicates only one session was performed. The duplicate charge should be removed.
typical_outcome: Removal of the duplicate dialysis charge.

summary: Modifier 25 was appended to an E/M service when a procedure was performed the same day, but the documentation did not support a significant, separately identifiable E/M beyond the work of the procedure. The note was focused on the procedure itself and did not describe a distinct evaluation (e.g., new problem or decision to perform the procedure) that would justify both the E/M and the procedure.
recommended_actions: Review note for separate E/M; confirm modifier 25 criteria and payer policy.
evidence_requests: Office note, procedure note, documentation of separate E/M.
evidence_checklist: Was there a separate problem addressed in addition to the procedure?
Does the note document history, exam, or MDM beyond the procedure?
Would the E/M have been billed if the procedure was not done?
letter_snippet: Modifier 25 was used to bill an E/M in addition to the procedure, but the documentation does not support a significant, separately identifiable E/M service. The E/M charge should be reversed.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the E/M charge or removal of modifier 25.

summary: A surgical tray or supply charge (e.g., A4550 or similar) was billed in addition to a procedure that already includes routine supplies in its global or facility fee. Many payers consider surgical trays and routine supplies to be part of the procedure and do not allow separate billing unless there is a specific, non-routine supply (e.g., implant) that is separately payable.
recommended_actions: Check payer policy on surgical tray and routine supplies; request itemized supply list.
evidence_requests: Procedure note, itemized supply charges, payer policy on surgical tray.
evidence_checklist: Does the payer allow separate surgical tray billing?
Were non-routine supplies used and documented?
Is the tray included in the facility or procedure fee?
letter_snippet: A surgical tray (or routine supply) charge was billed in addition to the procedure. Per payer policy, routine supplies are included in the procedure fee. This charge should be removed.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the surgical tray or routine supply charge.

summary: An abdominal or pelvic ultrasound was billed twice for the same date—for example, as a complete and a limited study, or as two separate exams—when the radiology report described a single examination. Duplicate ultrasound billing can occur when the same study is coded under two different codes or when the same service is entered twice on the claim.
recommended_actions: Request radiology report and order; confirm one exam vs. two distinct studies.
evidence_requests: Ultrasound report, order, technician worksheet.
evidence_checklist: Does the report describe one exam or two?
Were two separate body areas or indications documented?
Is the same timestamp or encounter on both charges?
letter_snippet: Two ultrasound charges appear for the same date of service, but the radiology report describes a single examination. The duplicate charge should be removed.
typical_outcome: Removal of the duplicate ultrasound charge.

summary: A new patient visit (e.g., 99203) was billed when the patient had been seen by the same provider or same group within the last three years, making them an established patient (99213–99215). Billing as new when the patient is established results in a higher payment and is incorrect per CMS and payer rules defining new vs. established patient.
recommended_actions: Verify prior visits with same provider/group/specialty within 3 years; request scheduling or prior encounter history.
evidence_requests: Prior encounter history, same tax ID or group, scheduling record.
evidence_checklist: Was the patient seen by this provider or group in the last 3 years?
Same specialty and same group per CMS definition?
Does the encounter note reference prior care by this provider?
letter_snippet: This visit was billed as a new patient (99203), but the patient had been seen by this provider (or same group/specialty) within the past three years. The visit should be billed as established (99213) with a corresponding charge adjustment.
typical_outcome: Rebilling as established patient; refund of overpayment.

summary: Respiratory therapy treatments (e.g., CPT 94640 or 94644) were billed multiple times for the same date when the therapy record showed fewer treatments or a single continuous treatment. Unit-based respiratory billing can lead to overbilling when the number of units does not match the documented number of treatments or duration.
recommended_actions: Request respiratory therapy flow sheet and order; reconcile units billed to treatments documented.
evidence_requests: Respiratory therapy record, physician order, MAR or treatment log.
evidence_checklist: How many treatments were documented for the date?
What is the billing unit (per treatment vs. per 15 min)?
Do the billed units match the record?
letter_snippet: Respiratory therapy was billed for more treatments than documented in the therapy record. The number of units should be reduced to match the documented treatments.
typical_outcome: Reduction of respiratory therapy units to match documentation.

summary: Blood product administration (e.g., transfusion) was billed with a facility or professional fee that substantially exceeded the typical rate, or the blood product (e.g., J-codes for blood) was billed at a markup far above cost. Blood product billing is subject to reasonable and customary limits; excessive admin fees or product markups can be disputed using CMS and payer benchmarks.
recommended_actions: Compare admin fee and product charge to CMS and blood bank cost; request itemized transfusion charges.
evidence_requests: Transfusion record, itemized charge for product and admin, blood bank invoice.
evidence_checklist: Is the administration fee above the CMS rate?
Is the blood product charge above cost or benchmark?
Were multiple units billed when only one was given?
letter_snippet: The blood transfusion administration and/or product charge exceeds reasonable and customary benchmarks. We request a reduction to align with CMS and typical payer rates.
typical_outcome: Reduction of admin or product charge to benchmark.

summary: Wound debridement was billed as a separate procedure in addition to another surgical procedure (e.g., same site or same encounter) when the debridement was part of or bundled with the primary procedure. NCCI and global surgery rules often include debridement when it is performed as part of the same surgical session or wound care; separate billing may require distinct documentation and modifier.
recommended_actions: Check NCCI for debridement and primary procedure; request procedure note and wound documentation.
evidence_requests: Procedure note, wound care note, order for debridement.
evidence_checklist: Was debridement at the same site as another billed procedure?
Is debridement bundled with the primary code per NCCI?
Was a modifier used and is it documented?
letter_snippet: Wound debridement was billed separately from the related procedure, but NCCI edits indicate these services are bundled. The separate debridement charge should be removed unless distinct documentation and modifier support it.
typical_outcome: Reversal of the separately billed debridement.

summary: A consultation (99242–99245 or 99252–99255) was billed when the encounter did not meet the criteria for a consultation: no written request from the requesting provider, or no written report sent back to the requesting provider. Many payers have eliminated or restricted consultation codes and require a referral and report; billing a consult when the criteria are not met can result in denial or downcode to a regular E/M.
recommended_actions: Verify referral request and consultant report; confirm payer still accepts consult codes.
evidence_requests: Referral request from requesting provider, consultant report sent to referring provider, payer policy on consultations.
evidence_checklist: Was there a written request for consultation?
Was a written report sent to the requesting provider?
Does the payer recognize consultation codes?
letter_snippet: A consultation was billed, but the encounter did not meet the criteria for a consultation (request from another provider and written report back). The visit should be billed as a standard E/M (99214 or equivalent) with a corresponding charge adjustment.
typical_outcome: Rebilling as E/M visit; refund of overpayment.

summary: An ambulatory surgery center (ASC) or same-day surgery charge included a facility fee that was significantly higher than the Medicare ASC rate or the rate for the same procedure at a competing ASC. ASC facility fees can vary by ownership and geography; when the billed amount is an outlier compared to CMS ASC rates and transparency data, the fee can be disputed.
recommended_actions: Compare ASC facility fee to CMS ASC rate and local benchmarks; request transparency data.
evidence_requests: Itemized ASC facility charge, CMS ASC payment rate for the procedure, ASC transparency file.
evidence_checklist: Is the facility fee above 2x the Medicare ASC rate?
How does this ASC rate compare to other ASCs in the area?
Was the procedure performed in an ASC or HOPD?
letter_snippet: The ambulatory surgery center facility fee for this procedure substantially exceeds the Medicare ASC rate and typical market rates. We request a reduction to a reasonable and customary amount.
typical_outcome: Negotiated reduction of ASC facility fee.

summary: A lipid panel and a basic metabolic panel were both billed on the same date when a comprehensive metabolic panel (which includes both) was also billed, or when only one draw was performed for overlapping tests. Overlapping lab panels result in duplicate billing for the same analytes; the more comprehensive panel typically supersedes the smaller ones when drawn from the same specimen.
recommended_actions: Compare panels ordered to panels billed; confirm one draw and one set of results.
evidence_requests: Lab orders, lab results, specimen collection time.
evidence_checklist: Which panels were ordered by the physician?
Does the CMP include the same analytes as the BMP and lipid?
Was one blood draw used for multiple panels?
letter_snippet: Multiple overlapping lab panels (e.g., CMP, BMP, lipid) were billed for the same date. When a comprehensive panel was performed, the component panels should not be billed separately. The duplicate panel charges should be removed.
typical_outcome: Removal of overlapping panel charges; retain only the comprehensive or appropriate panel.
